epigraph.quote: Our focus is not simply to add more products to the portfolio, but to develop value-added products that meet specific customer requirements in terms of purity, consistency and application performance.
epigraph.author: Hemango Gupta, Chief Executive Officer, Q2 FY27 call [6]

web_blocks.text: TANFAC describes a single fluorine-chemicals operating segment in India; its audited FY26 accounts say there is no reportable primary or secondary segment. Neither the annual report nor the supplied results provide product-level revenue or profit splits. Accordingly, the portfolio table below describes uses and operating status, not a product contribution ranking. The FY26 annual report separately says about 95% of revenue was domestic and 5% export; that is a geographic split, not a product mix. [1]

web_blocks.caption: Product applications and disclosed financial attribution. “Not separately reported” means the company has not disclosed product-level revenue/profit mix in the supplied filings. [1][2][4][5][6][7]
rows: Anhydrous HF (AHF) and ordinary diluted HF (DHF)

AHF is a feedstock for refrigerants, fluorinated organics and selected battery, pharmaceutical and agrochemical processes; diluted HF is used in steel pickling, glass/display processing and other surface treatment.
Core products from the Cuddalore platform; company reported about 30,000 TPA HF capacity and 95% utilization in FY26. [1][2]
Not separately reported. [1]
Solar-grade DHF
High-purity etching and cleaning of silicon wafers in photovoltaic-cell manufacture; disclosed purity specification is below 10 parts per billion for impurities.
Both original phases commissioned in FY26; order coverage was reported at about 85% of annual capacity through FY29. Capacity was later debottlenecked to 25,000 TPA by Q2 FY27. [1][2][4][5]
Not separately reported. [1]
Specialty inorganic fluorides

KF for fluorination in organic synthesis; potassium bifluoride for fluorine cells and brazing flux; BF3 complexes as catalysts; aluminium fluoride in aluminium smelting; sodium silicofluoride in ceramics, abrasives and glass.
Five-thousand-TPA aggregate specialty-fluoride capacity and 41% utilization in FY26; Q2 FY27 disclosures describe new products entering early commercialization. [1][2][6]
Not separately reported. [1]
Sulphuric acid and oleum
Captive input to HF production; surplus is sold into fertilizer, pulp, sulphonation and other industrial uses.
Reported capacity of 100,000 TPA and 101% utilization in FY26; captive power and waste-heat recovery support the integrated site. [1][2]
Not separately reported. [1]
HFC-32 / R-32 refrigerant gas
Refrigerant for residential split air conditioning and light-commercial HVAC; company describes it as a lower-GWP single-component option among widely used refrigerants.
20,000-TPA project under construction, with Q3 FY27 commissioning targeted; customer supply agreements were described as covering about 67.5% of planned annual capacity. [1][3][7]
No operating revenue or profit mix reported while the facility remained under construction. [1][6]

web_blocks.text: Think of a solar-wafer maker that needs clean wafers. TANFAC makes HF at Cuddalore, then purifies and dilutes some of it into solar-grade DHF. The buyer tests samples before approving regular supply. The chemical cleans and etches silicon wafers. TANFAC reports trials and orders, but does not name this buyer or give its shipment size. This is an example of the process, not a named account. [1][2][3]

An air-conditioner maker needs refrigerant with stable quality. TANFAC plans to make R-32 at Cuddalore from its fluorine platform. Company reports describe long-term supply deals. The November call says customer tests and plant readiness are still in progress. No buyer or contract price is public. This is an example, not a named customer. [1][6][7]

web_blocks.title: Mix disclosure boundary
paragraphs: Do not allocate group revenue, gross profit or EBITDA to AHF, solar-grade DHF, specialty fluorides, sulphuric acid or HFC-32 from capacity, order values or market sizes. The audited accounts disclose one operating segment, not those product-level economics. [1]

web_blocks.text: The portfolio is easiest to understand as a process map, not a list of independent businesses. Sulphuric acid and oleum support HF production; HF is then sold in anhydrous or diluted form, or converted to solar-grade DHF and specialty fluorides. TANFAC’s FY26 report identifies the molecule as the common base for its downstream fluorine products. The same physical integration creates both advantage and allocation choices: HF consumed internally is not also available for merchant sale, while each conversion step has its own purity, specification and qualification requirements. No public product-level volume bridge tells us how TANFAC allocates every tonne among those uses. [1][2][6]

web_blocks.text: The annual report says TANFAC serves more than 105 clients in over ten countries. It does not show revenue by customer. On the FY26 call, management said some buyer names could not be shared under confidentiality agreements. Public filings do not let you measure customer concentration, repeat orders or approval time by product. [1][3]

Company presentations quote third-party estimates for fluorochemicals, HF, solar-grade DHF and HFC-32. These are market totals, not TANFAC sales. They cover many suppliers and uses. They do not show the company’s share, volume or price. Better evidence is plant capacity, utilization, customer approval, signed orders and audited results. TANFAC reports one operating segment, so product-level profit is not public. [1][2]

web_blocks.title: A category label is not a segment account
paragraphs: “Specialty fluorides” groups multiple chemistries, “HF” includes anhydrous and diluted grades, and solar-grade DHF consumes HF internally. Capacity across these linked stages cannot be added as if each were an independent finished-goods business. The source material does not provide the product-level reconciliation needed to estimate revenue or profit shares. [1][2][6]

web_blocks.text: That measurement boundary changes how you should interpret growth. A product can be strategically important without yet contributing material group profit; an internal intermediate can enable downstream sales while disappearing from external revenue; and a contract value may provide visibility without reporting volume delivery or margin. The company does not disclose enough to calculate customer-level retention, product-specific gross profit, or product-level working-capital intensity. The correct analytical choice is not to estimate a split from capacity or order value, but to explain what is known and mark the boundary. [1][2][3]

book_paragraphs: Think of the portfolio as a conversion ladder built around hydrofluoric acid. TANFAC starts with feedstocks and upstream acids, makes AHF and diluted grades, and uses part of that stream in products with tighter purity or application requirements. The ladder offers a credible route to value addition, but it is not a disclosed segment model: you cannot see audited product margins or identify which line contributes how much profit. The company explicitly reports one fluorine-chemicals operating segment. [1]

When you picture the customer, keep the example honest. A wafer-fabrication customer may need a high-purity chemical qualified for etching and cleaning; an HVAC manufacturer may need refrigerant supply and predictable specifications. These are end-market archetypes derived from disclosed applications, not claims about named TANFAC buyers. Long-term agreements and customer qualification matter, but they do not substitute for disclosed product-level revenue, realized margins, or shipment histories. [1][2][6]

Imagine a customer opening a process-qualification file rather than an investor presentation. A photovoltaic wafer maker needs an etchant and cleaner whose impurity profile is tight enough for its process. The product in the disclosed example is solar-grade diluted hydrofluoric acid. TANFAC begins with its captive HF capability, develops the required high-purity grade, submits samples for evaluation, and reports successful trials and certification with an Indian wafer manufacturer. The next commercial step is scheduled supply against orders that the company says extend through FY29. That is an end-to-end archetype grounded in public disclosures; the buyer is not named here, and the filings do not disclose shipment-level volumes, customer-specific timing or the resulting product margin. [1][2][3]

Now consider an HVAC producer as a second archetype. Its problem is refrigerant availability for room air-conditioning or light-commercial cooling. The exact planned product is HFC-32. TANFAC intends to make it at Cuddalore using its fluorine platform, with an announced 20,000-tonne annual facility and a stated Q3 FY27 commissioning target. The management call discusses qualification and customer evaluation, and the company reports long-term supply arrangements covering a portion of planned capacity. Formula-based arrangements pass through raw-material movements over a defined period, but the public evidence does not disclose every contract term, the buyers protected by confidentiality, or the product’s operating margin. Do not present the planned workflow as a current shipment. [1][3][6][7]

The steel, glass, pharmaceutical and agrochemical examples are useful for understanding applications, but they do not create a product-level income statement. Potassium fluoride is a fluorinating agent; BF3 complexes act as catalysts; aluminium fluoride is used in aluminium smelting; sodium silicofluoride has industrial uses in glass, ceramics and abrasives. Industrial diluted HF serves pickling and surface treatment. The disclosures establish that these products exist and identify some uses. They do not tell you which one produces the highest contribution, whether a customer relationship is exclusive, or the length of an individual approval cycle. [1][2]

This is where analytical restraint becomes part of the work. TANFAC reports a single fluorine-chemicals segment in India. The 95% domestic and 5% export split is geographic, not a product split; capacity is not revenue; order value is not profit; and internal consumption of HF is not an external sale. You may discuss the strategic route from feedstock to higher-purity grades and the market applications, but you cannot allocate group profits among these lines without data the company has not supplied. [1]

When a company presents many product names, you may feel that diversification is already proven. Pause and ask whether the names correspond to independent economics. TANFAC’s product ladder shares HF as a core molecule; some HF is captive feedstock, and several specialty fluorides sit within a single aggregate capacity category. That arrangement can produce genuine operating synergies, but it also means capacity figures overlap in the chemistry chain. The company’s one-segment disclosure is the financial boundary you have to respect. Until product-level sales and profit reporting appears, describe the portfolio breadth without manufacturing a contribution ranking. [1][2]

The archetypes also help you identify what would count as evidence. For the wafer customer, later confirmation could include repeat orders, capacity utilization after debottlenecking, timely delivery and collection of receivables. For the HVAC customer, evidence begins after plant commissioning and buyer qualification; it then extends to actual output, reliable specifications and recurring supply. The company has described formula pass-through with a lag, but not every term or buyer. In each case, a successful first trial is encouraging, but it does not answer whether the product scales or earns an attractive contribution. Keep the workflow customer-centered and the outcome evidence-based. [1][2][3][6]

For a buyer, a chemical specification is part of the product, not a decorative label. Management emphasizes purity, consistency and application performance, and the solar-grade disclosure gives a concrete high-purity use case. That tells you why technical qualification can shape the commercial relationship. It does not tell you how long each customer approval takes, what rejection rates are, or how much additional service is required per molecule. Treat qualification as a process capability supported by the reported trials, and use repeat commercial supply as the next evidence. This preserves the customer’s perspective without inventing procurement terms or buyer identities. [1][2][6]

A product taxonomy is useful only when its categories remain stable. The annual report’s portfolio table describes applications molecule by molecule, while the financial statements consolidate them into one fluorine-chemicals segment. Later presentations add products and variants, but do not turn those additions into separately reported businesses. This means the product map can help you understand technical adjacency and customer need, while the audited segment note governs financial attribution. If product names change or the portfolio expands, compare the reporting boundary first; do not infer a new revenue stream simply because a new item appears in a presentation. [1][2][4]

book_callouts.title: Reflection — product story versus product economics
book_callouts.text: For each product, can you identify the use case, the operating status, and a disclosed revenue or profit contribution? Here the first two are documented for several lines; product-specific financial attribution is not. Do not fill that gap with capacity or order value. [1]
